title: Heat capacity, calorimetry and phase changes
voiceInstructions: Warm, engaging female teacher with a natural General American English accent. Relaxed, welcoming and lightly playful, with a gentle smile and conversational rhythm. Keep scientific terms precise and avoid an announcer cadence. Slow down for equations, numbers and conversions. Give brief natural thinking pauses after questions. Do not add words or laughter absent from the script.

sources.title: NTA: Official JEE Main 2026 syllabus, Physics Unit 7

chapters.title: Heat is transfer, not temperature
chapters.formula: Q = m c Delta T; heat capacity C = m c
points: Heat transfers energy because of a temperature difference.
Specific heat c has unit J/(kg K); heat capacity C has unit J/K.
Heating 0.5 kg of water by 10 K with c = 4200 J/(kg K) requires 21 kJ.
chapters.script: Hey, welcome back. Imagine a small cup of warm water and a large bucket at exactly the same temperature. Does warming them by ten degrees require the same energy? Of course not. The bucket contains much more water. Temperature is not a measure of how much energy we must supply. Heat means energy transferred because of a temperature difference. Internal energy belongs to the system; heat describes a transfer. For a solid or liquid with approximately constant specific heat and no change of phase, the energy supplied is mass times specific heat times temperature change. Specific heat tells us how much energy one kilogram needs for a one kelvin rise. Heat capacity belongs to the whole sample, so it is mass times specific heat. Let's heat half a kilogram of water by ten kelvin, using a given specific heat of four thousand two hundred joules per kilogram per kelvin. Half times four thousand two hundred times ten is twenty one thousand joules, or twenty one kilojoules. Double the mass and we need twice the energy. Use the temperature change, not the final temperature. A change in degrees Celsius has the same numerical value in kelvin. This equation describes sensible heating; we need a different term when a substance melts or boils.

chapters.title: Mixing: balance energy, not temperatures
chapters.formula: Heat lost = heat gained; sum of m c (Tf - Ti) = 0
points: Assume an insulated mixture with no phase change or significant work.
For the same substance, mass-weighted temperature replaces a simple average.
0.2 kg water at 80 C mixed with 0.3 kg at 20 C reaches 44 C.
chapters.script: Now let's mix hot and cold water in an insulated cup. We assume no evaporation, no phase change and negligible energy absorbed by the cup for this first example. The hot water loses energy and the cold water gains the same amount. That is conservation of energy, not a rule about simply averaging two temperatures. Mix zero point two kilograms of water at eighty degrees Celsius with zero point three kilograms at twenty degrees Celsius. Call the final temperature T. The hot sample loses zero point two times c times eighty minus T. The cold sample gains zero point three times c times T minus twenty. Equate them. Since both samples are water, the same specific heat cancels. We get sixteen minus zero point two T equals zero point three T minus six. So twenty two equals zero point five T, giving forty four degrees Celsius. Pause and check whether that is sensible. It lies between twenty and eighty, and it is closer to twenty because there is more cold water. The simple average, fifty degrees, would be wrong. For different substances, weight the temperatures by their heat capacities, mass times specific heat, rather than by mass alone. A final temperature outside the initial temperature range is a warning sign in this simple mixing model.

chapters.title: The calorimeter also absorbs energy
chapters.formula: mHot cHot (Thot - Tf) = (mWater cWater + Ccup)(Tf - Tcold)
points: Include the vessel if its heat capacity is not negligible.
Water equivalent = vessel heat capacity / water specific heat.
A 0.1 kg metal sample with c = 400 cooling from 100 to 30 C releases 2800 J.
chapters.script: Our cup was ignored in the last problem. Real calorimeters also change temperature, so let's give the cup its share of the energy. Suppose a hot metal sample is placed in cooler water and both water and cup begin at the same temperature. The metal's energy loss must warm the water and the cup together. Add the water's heat capacity to the cup's heat capacity before multiplying by their temperature rise. Here is a compact example. A zero point one kilogram metal sample has specific heat four hundred joules per kilogram per kelvin. It cools from one hundred to thirty degrees Celsius. Its heat capacity is forty joules per kelvin, and a seventy kelvin fall releases two thousand eight hundred joules. If the water has heat capacity two hundred and forty joules per kelvin, and the cup has forty, their combined heat capacity is two hundred and eighty. Starting at twenty degrees, they need two hundred and eighty times ten, again two thousand eight hundred joules, to reach thirty degrees. The energy balance checks. You may see a calorimeter described by its water equivalent. That is the mass of water with the same heat capacity as the vessel: divide the vessel's heat capacity by water's specific heat. It is a convenient comparison, not extra water secretly inside the apparatus.

chapters.title: Latent heat and the heating curve
chapters.formula: Q = m L during a phase change; add m c Delta T between transitions
points: A pure substance can absorb energy at constant temperature during melting or boiling at fixed pressure.
Specific latent heat L has unit J/kg.
Heating 0.1 kg ice from -10 C to water at 20 C needs 2.1 + 33.4 + 8.4 = 43.9 kJ with the stated constants.
chapters.script: Can a substance absorb energy without becoming hotter? Yes. During melting or boiling of a pure substance at fixed pressure, energy changes its phase while the temperature stays at the transition value. That is why a heating curve has plateaus. The required energy is mass times the specific latent heat. Let's turn ice at minus ten degrees Celsius into water at twenty degrees. Take mass zero point one kilograms, ice specific heat two thousand one hundred, fusion latent heat three hundred and thirty four thousand joules per kilogram, and water specific heat four thousand two hundred. There are three stages. First warm the ice by ten kelvin: two point one kilojoules. Next melt it at zero degrees: thirty three point four kilojoules. Finally warm the melted water by twenty kelvin: eight point four kilojoules. Add them to get forty three point nine kilojoules. Don't multiply the ice specific heat by the entire thirty degree interval. The material changes phase, and its specific heat changes too. For steam that condenses and then cools, include the condensation energy before cooling the liquid. The plateau rule assumes the stated pressure and a pure substance; it is not a universal claim that every material changes phase at one fixed temperature.

chapters.title: Ice mixtures: check whether all the ice melts
chapters.formula: Compare available cooling energy with mIce L before solving for Tf
points: If energy is insufficient for melting all ice, equilibrium may be an ice-water mixture at 0 C.
0.1 kg water at 20 C releases 8400 J on cooling to 0 C.
With 0.05 kg ice initially at 0 C, approximately 0.02515 kg melts; the rest remains.
chapters.script: Here's the step that saves many ice mixture questions: check the phase before solving for the final temperature. Place zero point zero five kilograms of ice at zero degrees into zero point one kilograms of water at twenty degrees, in an insulated container of negligible heat capacity. Use water specific heat four thousand two hundred and fusion latent heat three hundred and thirty four thousand. Cooling the water to zero releases eight thousand four hundred joules. Melting all the ice would require sixteen thousand seven hundred joules. There isn't enough energy. So the equilibrium is at zero degrees, with some ice still present. Divide eight thousand four hundred by three hundred and thirty four thousand. About zero point zero two five one five kilograms, or twenty five point one five grams, melts. Roughly twenty four point eight five grams remains as ice. A calculation that assumes all the ice melts might produce a negative liquid water temperature. That is a signal to revisit the assumed final state, not to accept the impossible result. If available energy exceeds the melting requirement, subtract the latent heat first, then use the remaining energy to warm all the liquid water. Always account for the container if its heat capacity is given. Energy balance plus a phase check is the heart of calorimetry.
